cases.sentence: ___ протягивает морду, тяжело вздыхает и умирает.
options: кляча
клячи
кляче
клячей
cases.translation: The old nag stretches out her muzzle, sighs heavily, and dies.
cases.explain: "Кляча" is the subject of the verbs "протягивает," "вздыхает," and "умирает," so it stands in the nominative case.

cases.sentence: …но дойдя уже до Петровского ___, остановился в полном изнеможении…
options: остров
острова
острову
островом
cases.translation: …but having already reached Petrovsky Island, he stopped in complete exhaustion…
cases.explain: The preposition "до" (as far as/until) governs the genitive case, giving "острова."

cases.sentence: …он хотел было поворотить назад, к ___, но домой идти ему стало вдруг ужасно противно.
options: дом
дома
дому
домом
cases.translation: …he wanted to turn back toward home, but going home suddenly became terribly repugnant to him.
cases.explain: The preposition "к" (toward) always governs the dative case, giving "дому."

cases.sentence: Он бросил ___ и пошел, почти побежал.
options: скамейка
скамейки
скамейке
скамейку
cases.translation: He abandoned the bench and walked, almost ran.
cases.explain: The transitive verb "бросил" (left/abandoned) governs the accusative case for its direct object, giving "скамейку."

cases.sentence: Он лет семи и гуляет в праздничный день, под вечер, с своим ___ за городом.
options: отец
отца
отцу
отцом
cases.translation: He is about seven years old and is walking on a holiday, toward evening, with his father outside town.
cases.explain: The preposition "с" (with) governs the instrumental case, giving "отцом."

cases.sentence: …он пошел домой; но дойдя уже до Петровского острова, остановился в полном ___, сошел с дороги, вошел в кусты, пал на траву и в ту же минуту заснул.
options: изнеможение
изнеможения
изнеможению
изнеможении
cases.translation: …he headed home, but having reached Petrovsky Island, he stopped in complete exhaustion, stepped off the road, went into the bushes, fell on the grass, and fell asleep that instant.
cases.explain: The preposition "в" describing a state governs the prepositional case, giving "изнеможении."

reading.ru: Право, смешно, что я пошел к Разумихину…
reading.question: How does Raskolnikov judge his own impulse to visit Razumikhin?
options: He finds it genuinely funny/absurd that he went to see him
He considers it his most logical decision
He feels proud of the idea
He thinks it was planned long in advance
reading.correct: He finds it genuinely funny/absurd that he went to see him
reading.explain: He admits to himself that it is really funny that he went to Razumikhin, showing his confusion about his own motives.

reading.ru: Что ж, неужели я всё дело хотел поправить одним Разумихиным и всему исход нашел в Разумихине?»
reading.question: What question does Raskolnikov ask himself with astonishment?
options: Whether he really wanted to fix his whole situation through Razumikhin alone
Whether Razumikhin has betrayed him
Whether he should abandon his studies entirely
Whether Razumikhin needs his help instead
reading.correct: Whether he really wanted to fix his whole situation through Razumikhin alone
reading.explain: He asks himself in astonishment whether he really wanted to solve his whole problem through Razumikhin alone.

reading.ru: к Разумихину я пойду, это конечно… но — не теперь…
reading.question: When does Raskolnikov decide he will actually go see Razumikhin?
options: Not now, but only after "that" is finished and everything is different
Immediately, without delay
Only after he finds a new job
Never — he decides against it entirely
reading.correct: Not now, but only after "that" is finished and everything is different
reading.explain: He decides he will go to Razumikhin eventually, but not now — only afterward, once "that" is over and everything has changed.

reading.ru: он хотел было поворотить назад, к дому, но домой идти ему стало вдруг ужасно противно
reading.question: Why doesn't Raskolnikov turn back toward home?
options: Because going home suddenly became terribly repugnant to him
Because his landlady had locked the door
Because he forgot the way
Because a friend stopped him on the street
reading.correct: Because going home suddenly became terribly repugnant to him
reading.explain: He wants to turn back toward home, but going home suddenly feels terribly repugnant to him, associated with his tormenting plan.

reading.ru: Ноги его вдруг отяжелели, и он начал чувствовать сильный позыв ко сну.
reading.question: What physical effect does the vodka have on Raskolnikov?
options: His legs suddenly grow heavy and he feels a strong urge to sleep
He feels a burst of new energy
He becomes nauseated and vomits
He feels no effect at all
reading.correct: His legs suddenly grow heavy and he feels a strong urge to sleep
reading.explain: After drinking the vodka, his legs suddenly grow heavy and he starts to feel a strong urge to sleep.

reading.ru: Он пошел домой; но дойдя уже до Петровского острова, остановился в полном изнеможении, сошел с дороги, вошел в кусты, пал на траву и в ту же минуту заснул.
reading.question: Where does Raskolnikov end up falling asleep?
options: In the bushes near Petrovsky Island, having collapsed from exhaustion
In his own bed at home
On a bench in a public park
Inside a tavern
reading.correct: In the bushes near Petrovsky Island, having collapsed from exhaustion
reading.explain: Heading home, upon reaching Petrovsky Island he stops from exhaustion, steps into the bushes, falls on the grass, and falls asleep instantly.

reading.ru: Страшный сон приснился Раскольникову.
reading.question: What happens to Raskolnikov as he sleeps in the bushes?
options: He has a terrible dream
He is woken by a policeman
He sleeps peacefully without dreaming
He is robbed while unconscious
reading.correct: He has a terrible dream
reading.explain: The text states plainly that a terrible dream came to Raskolnikov.

reading.ru: Он лет семи и гуляет в праздничный день, под вечер, с своим отцом за городом.
reading.question: What does Raskolnikov dream about regarding his childhood?
options: Himself as a seven-year-old boy walking with his father outside town on a holiday
His university graduation ceremony
His first day pawning items at Alyona Ivanovna's
A trip to Petersburg with his mother
reading.correct: Himself as a seven-year-old boy walking with his father outside town on a holiday
reading.explain: He dreams of his childhood: himself at about age seven, walking with his father outside their small town on a holiday evening.

reading.ru: Папочка, папочка, — кричит он отцу, — папочка, что они делают? Папочка, бедную лошадку бьют!
reading.question: What does the boy in the dream cry out to his father in distress?
options: That they are beating the poor little horse
That he wants to go home immediately
That he is hungry
That he is afraid of the drunk men
reading.correct: That they are beating the poor little horse
reading.explain: The boy cries out to his father, asking what they are doing, horrified that they are beating the poor little horse.

reading.ru: Секи до смерти! — кричит Миколка, — на то пошло. Засеку!
reading.question: What does Mikolka shout as he continues to beat the exhausted horse?
options: That he will whip it to death, since it's come to that
That he will stop beating it now
That he needs help lifting the cart
That the horse should be set free
reading.correct: That he will whip it to death, since it's come to that
reading.explain: In his fury, Mikolka shouts that he will whip her to death, since it has come to that.

reading.ru: Кляча протягивает морду, тяжело вздыхает и умирает.
reading.question: What happens to the horse at the climax of the dream?
options: She stretches out her muzzle, sighs heavily, and dies
She breaks free and runs away
She suddenly becomes strong again
She is rescued by the boy's father
reading.correct: She stretches out her muzzle, sighs heavily, and dies
reading.explain: The dream reaches its horrifying climax as the poor nag stretches out her muzzle, sighs heavily, and dies.

reading.ru: Он обхватывает отца руками, но грудь ему теснит, теснит.
reading.question: What happens to the boy just as the dream ends?
options: He clings to his father, but his chest feels crushed and tight
He runs away from his father in anger
He falls asleep peacefully in his father's arms
He begins laughing hysterically
reading.correct: He clings to his father, but his chest feels crushed and tight
reading.explain: As the dream ends, the boy clings to his father, but his chest feels increasingly tight and constricted, just before he wakes.

reading.ru: Он проснулся весь в поту, с мокрыми от поту волосами, задыхаясь, и приподнялся в ужасе.
reading.question: In what state does Raskolnikov wake from his nightmare?
options: Covered in sweat, gasping for breath, and rising up in horror
Perfectly calm and refreshed
Still fast asleep and unaware
Laughing at the absurdity of the dream
reading.correct: Covered in sweat, gasping for breath, and rising up in horror
reading.explain: He wakes drenched in sweat, his hair wet with it, gasping, and sits up in terror.

reading.ru: «Слава богу, это только сон! — сказал он, садясь под деревом и глубоко переводя дыхание.
reading.question: What does Raskolnikov say to reassure himself right after waking?
options: "Thank God, it was only a dream!"
"This must be a sign from God"
"I must tell Razumikhin at once"
"I am going mad for certain"
reading.correct: "Thank God, it was only a dream!"
reading.explain: Sitting under a tree and catching his breath, he exclaims with relief, "Thank God, it's only a dream!"

reading.ru: «Боже! — воскликнул он, — да неужели ж, неужели ж я в самом деле возьму топор, стану бить по голове, размозжу ей череп…
reading.question: What horrifying possibility does Raskolnikov confront directly after the dream?
options: That he might really take an axe and smash her skull with it
That he might be arrested that very night
That his mother might disown him
That Razumikhin might discover his plan
reading.correct: That he might really take an axe and smash her skull with it
reading.explain: He cries out to God in horror, questioning whether he could really take up an axe and smash her skull.

reading.ru: Нет, я не вытерплю, не вытерплю!
reading.question: What does Raskolnikov repeatedly insist to himself after the nightmare?
options: That he will not be able to endure it, he simply cannot go through with it
That he must act immediately without hesitation
That he no longer cares about the consequences
That the plan is now easier than ever
reading.correct: That he will not be able to endure it, he simply cannot go through with it
reading.explain: He repeats emphatically that he will not endure it — he cannot bring himself to carry out the deed.

reading.ru: «Господи! — молил он, — покажи мне путь мой, а я отрекаюсь от этой проклятой… мечты моей!»
reading.question: What prayer does Raskolnikov make as he feels relieved of his burden?
options: He begs God to show him his path and renounces his cursed dream
He prays for wealth and success
He prays that Luzhin will die
He prays to be forgiven for a crime already committed
reading.correct: He begs God to show him his path and renounces his cursed dream
reading.explain: He prays to God to show him his path, declaring that he renounces this accursed dream of his.

reading.ru: Свобода, свобода! Он свободен теперь от этих чар, от колдовства, обаяния, от наваждения!
reading.question: How does Raskolnikov feel as he crosses the bridge after his prayer?
options: Free — free from the charms, sorcery, fascination, and obsession that gripped him
Utterly hopeless and trapped
Angry at himself for weakness
Indifferent to everything around him
reading.correct: Free — free from the charms, sorcery, fascination, and obsession that gripped him
reading.explain: He exults inwardly, feeling free at last from the spell, sorcery, fascination, and obsession that had gripped him for so long.

reading.ru: Было около девяти часов, когда он проходил по Сенной.
reading.question: What time is it when Raskolnikov walks through Sennaya Square?
options: About nine o'clock
Midnight
Early morning, around six
Noon
reading.correct: About nine o'clock
reading.explain: The narrator notes it was around nine o'clock when he passed through Sennaya (Haymarket) Square.

reading.ru: Раскольников преимущественно любил эти места, равно как и все близлежащие переулки, когда выходил без цели на улицу.
reading.question: Why does Raskolnikov particularly like Sennaya Square and its side streets?
options: Because his ragged clothes drew no special attention there when he wandered aimlessly
Because his favorite bookstore is located there
Because his mother used to live nearby
Because it reminds him of his university days
reading.correct: Because his ragged clothes drew no special attention there when he wandered aimlessly
reading.explain: The text explains he especially loved these places (as noted just before) because his rags drew no haughty attention there when he went out aimlessly.

reading.ru: Знакомая эта была Лизавета Ивановна, или просто, как все звали ее, Лизавета, младшая сестра той самой старухи Алены Ивановны
reading.question: Who does Raskolnikov recognize speaking with the tradesman and his wife?
options: Lizaveta Ivanovna, the younger sister of the pawnbroker Alyona Ivanovna
Katerina Ivanovna, Marmeladov's wife
His own sister, Dunya
The landlady, Praskovya Pavlovna
reading.correct: Lizaveta Ivanovna, the younger sister of the pawnbroker Alyona Ivanovna
reading.explain: The acquaintance turns out to be Lizaveta Ivanovna, known simply as Lizaveta, the younger sister of old Alyona Ivanovna the pawnbroker.

reading.ru: — Хорошо, приду, — проговорила Лизавета, всё еще раздумывая, и медленно стала с места трогаться.
reading.question: What does Lizaveta finally agree to, still hesitating?
options: To come to the tradesman's the next day at seven in the evening
To sell her sister's belongings immediately
To move in with the tradesman's family
To refuse the tradesman's offer entirely
reading.correct: To come to the tradesman's the next day at seven in the evening
reading.explain: Still hesitant, Lizaveta agrees, saying "All right, I'll come," and slowly starts to move off, confirming the appointment for seven the next evening.

reading.ru: Он узнал, он вдруг, внезапно и совершенно неожиданно узнал, что завтра, ровно в семь часов вечера, Лизаветы, старухиной сестры и единственной ее сожительницы, дома не будет и что, стало быть, старуха, ровно в семь часов вечера, останется дома одна.
reading.question: What crucial piece of information does Raskolnikov overhear and immediately grasp?
options: That tomorrow at exactly seven in the evening, Lizaveta will be away and the old woman will be home alone
That the old woman is planning to move away permanently
That Lizaveta is planning to report him to the police
That the old woman has already sold all her valuables
reading.correct: That tomorrow at exactly seven in the evening, Lizaveta will be away and the old woman will be home alone
reading.explain: He suddenly and unexpectedly learns that at exactly seven the next evening, Lizaveta will be out, meaning the old woman will be home entirely alone.

reading.ru: До его квартиры оставалось только несколько шагов. Он вошел к себе, как приговоренный к смерти.
reading.question: How does Raskolnikov feel entering his room after overhearing this crucial detail?
options: Like a man condemned to death
Full of joy and relief
Completely indifferent
Excited and hopeful about the future
reading.correct: Like a man condemned to death
reading.explain: With only a few steps left to his lodging, he enters his room feeling like a man condemned to death, sensing his fate is sealed.

reading.ru: Конечно, если бы даже целые годы приходилось ему ждать удобного случая, то и тогда, имея замысел, нельзя было рассчитывать наверное, на более очевидный шаг к успеху этого замысла, как тот, который представлялся вдруг сейчас.
reading.question: How significant does the narrator suggest this chance discovery is for Raskolnikov's plan?
options: Even years of waiting could not have produced a more obvious step toward the plan's success than this sudden chance
It was ultimately meaningless and changed nothing
It made the plan much harder to carry out
It convinced him to abandon the plan forever
reading.correct: Even years of waiting could not have produced a more obvious step toward the plan's success than this sudden chance
reading.explain: The narrator remarks that even if he had waited whole years for a favorable opportunity, he could not have counted on a clearer step toward his plan's success than what had just presented itself by chance.
